“Where is the gospel?” or so I found myself asking all throughout. In what is ostensibly an apologetic, Nouwen seems to shy away from any mention of what makes the Christian life at all distinctive and worthwhile: the redemptive power of Christ on the cross. One is taken and adopted as a child of God, through Christ’s work. One is blessed and broken, as Christ was blessed and broken. One is given for others, because Christ first gave himself. Here the Eucharist is used as a framing device yet entirely emptied of its meaning and power. For one is beloved in the Beloved. It’s no surprise, then, to find that his friends found the book uncompelling; how could it, without the gospel? What might have been a tender testament to the salvation that comes only from above becomes only impotent word-wrangling and hollow mysticism.

page.description: One readily distinguishes between day and night. The two are revealed in their qualities: day is bright, generally speaking, and night is dark. But the same must contend with those troublesome periods called twilight. It is here that the one who thinks himself rather principled may begin to think: “Well, then there is evidently no true distinction between day and night.” If he knows something about the rotation of the earth, he may say that what we in casual speech call “day” and “night” denote only contrasting degrees of luminous flux from that aggregation of gases known as the Sun. But one properly cannot divide the two, and neither “day” nor “night” may be said to exist in the underlying reality.

In a thoroughly engaging biography of Luther, Bainton plants the reformer firmly in his own political and theological landscape: the final decades of the medieval age, and the age of the Renaissance and of nationalism. He traces Luther’s thought by way of the man’s own writings and those of his allies, his observers, and his enemies. Ample discussion of the personal and theological contemporaries supplements without distracting too much from Luther himself. The picture is complex; the man is variously polemic and deferential, sometimes unreservedly jocular, so much that occasional glimpses at his tenderness are startling. It is one of a titan of church history: a passionate theologian and a pastor, a musician and a prolific scholar, a father; above all, an intensely and painfully devotional Christian.

page.description: Canon Revisited argues that “God has created the proper epistemic environment wherein belief in the New Testament canon can be reliably formed.” Recall that the question at hand is the de jure objection: even supposing that the New Testament canon is true, how can Christians know that it is true? Truth does not necessarily confer epistemic access in general. But in this case, Scripture itself testifies to this epistemic environment. Unlike the externally authenticated models, which cannot authenticate the canon as the ultimate rule over the church, the self-authenticating canonical model properly grounds the Scripture, which bears the authority of God, who “[swears] by himself,” in itself as the ultimate authority.

page.description: Hellenistic thinkers appear to have conceived of reality in degrees of inferiority, in which a divine permanence and perpetuity occupies the summit of the hierarchy. The movement and change perceived in Time, then, is cyclical, for the identical recurrence of the same things—thus ensuring their survival—is the natural expression of that ultimate reality. The immediate reality is governed by its superior realities of increasing regularity in the cosmic order, the celestial bodies and luminaries, who are empowered by if not of divine natures. The consequences are immediate and severe: notions of past and present break down, because no event is unique but has occurred, occurs, and will occur again, eternally. There is neither beginning nor end, nor can one fathom any kind of continuous progress in between. Cities rise, corrupt, fall, and rise again. Troy was before yet after, and therefore always. History does not exist as such.

The tale of Orpheus and Eurydice as now popularly known ends in tragedy. The bereaved Orpheus descends into the underworld, harp or lyre in hand; there, he plays music so sweet as to move Charon, and Cerberus, and even Hades, that the king of the underworld grants him to take Eurydice back into the realm of the living, with the condition that he must not look backwards whilst they’re still in the nether’s darkness. In some versions, as in Virgil’s Gregorics (first century BCE), he forgets this charge; approaching the light of the living world, the joy-enraptured Orpheus looks to share his delight with Eurydice—and she’s taken away from him. Other accounts, as in Ovid’s Metamorphoses X (first century CE), suggest that he’s possessed by a fear that the gods have tricked him. Either way, the famous musician fails and returns alone, twice-robbed.

The language is delightful, but one can’t help but agree with Tolkien’s assessment that what underlies the entire saga is “an evil and indeed silly ‘philosophy’” and the ending has one wondering indeed if Eddison admired “arrogance and cruelty.”

page.description: Some months after reading this book I encountered a fellow in a bookshop who exclaimed that it was a life wasted. But I don’t think this is at all the picture. The life is not over! No, “I gave my best to Lord Darlington. I gave him the very best I had to give, and now—well—I find I do not have a great deal more left to give,” he says, speaking in relation to his present service to Mr Farraday; but surely he is also speaking of how, in giving all of himself to that image of a butler, he had little left to give to the others in his life: his father, his friends, and Miss Kenton. At least Darlington “chose a certain path in life,” though it “proved to be a misguided one,” whereas he “can’t even say [he] made [his] own mistakes.” He gave his very best, yet it was a giving marked by a passivity which let moments and opportunities slip by. He thought himself to be carrying out the duties of his post in proper dignity, yet now he laments, “Really—one has to ask oneself—what dignity is there in that?”

page.description: The so-called “‘Achilles’ heel’ of Protestant Christianity” is the problem of the canon: how can we know that we have the right books in the New Testament? If Christians, individually and corporately as the church, are called to dedicate their lives in their entirety to God and the gospel based on Bible, then it is certainly critical that those books which constitute that ultimate rule and authority actually be the inspired Word of God. But it seems that many things could go quite wrong. What if the books are not inspired, in whole or in part? What if there are inspired books missing from the canon? Even supposing that they are inspired, how could anyone know that they are? Is the Christian able to reasonably account for the origin and authority of his own canon?

Plenty of people have spoken or written about the enduring mystic of Skyrim. In spite of newer experiences which may boast gripping narratives or real-to-life visuals or delightful gameplay loops, those whose hearts upon which has lain the tender yet unyielding hold of idyllic Tamriel find themselves returning again and again, even nigh fifteen years now, to that northern corner of the world. By most reasonable measures the game’s combat mechanics are rather lacking; the quest writing varies from uninspired to abominable; the whole experience is rife with visual and functional deficiency and defect, of both comic and exasperating character. Yet somehow it is a spring from which all weariness seems to depart; when novelties have worn off, one remembers the rugged peak and the rolling pastures, the surly wanderer and the unassuming stableboy, the hidden cove and the homely home.

page.description: The latest issue of Mallorn has a nice article positing that Tom Bombadil represents Tolkien’s conception of an unfallen Adam. As the author mentions, the idea of an Adamic identity is not new, having appeared, apparently, in obscure fanzines from the 1970s, in Shippey’s The Road to Middle-Earth, and in a 2018 article by Jane Beal. But the author argues that Tom is not identical to Adam nor prelapsarian, as he doesn’t appear to be the progenitor of all man-kind and betrays none of Adam’s weakness; he embodies, instead, “an alternative Adam who never fell,” that is, “what would have happened had the serpent… failed”. I suppose I would wonder, then, why Tom has no progeny; this is the one point that seems incongruent with the divine command in Genesis 1:28: “And God said to them, ‘Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth,’” it says. Perhaps he just hasn’t yet gotten around to it.

page.description: From a friend of a friend I was recently introduced to the idea that Time might be conceived of as a delta. Our individual streams flow, sometimes slowly and sometimes quickly, winding. We cross with the streams of those around us, at times touching, mingling, exchanging; others we pass by, never to wander near again. We meet, and we depart. We experience, and remember. Even if we forget, that does not change the fact that it happened. If nothing else there is progress, that continuum of irreversible change.

Canon Revisited seeks to address the de jure objection to Christian belief in the inspiration and authority of the New Testament canon: even supposing that the belief is a true belief, Christians have no way of knowing that it is true. In other words, Christians are not warranted in holding the belief rationally, since there is no justification for it. Though the question may seem alarmingly circular—if one assumes that Scripture is inspired and authoritative, why is there need to justify it?—but that a statement is true is distinct from one’s knowing that it is true. It may be raining outside, but if I am in a deep underground cell where I cannot see the rain, hear the drops, nor feel the moisture, then it is another matter to say that I know it is raining. I may sincerely believe that it is raining (because I believe that my sneezing three times within a minute usually means it is raining), and I happen to be right in that moment, but arguably I cannot be said to know the fact. Truth does not necessarily imply epistemic access.
